los.text: Identify the major tracts of the brainstem in transverse section.
los.html:
LevelFront (ventral)MiddleBack (dorsal)
Midbrain (superior colliculus)Cerebral peduncles (corticospinal and corticobulbar), substantia nigra, CN III nucleus and fibres, red nucleusMedial lemniscus, spinothalamic tract (lateral)Cerebral aqueduct, periaqueductal grey, superior colliculi
PonsBasilar pons: corticospinal fibres broken up by pontine nuclei; transverse pontocerebellar fibresMedial lemniscus (now horizontal), spinothalamic, MLF, VI and VII nuclei4th ventricle floor
Medulla (open, upper)Pyramids (corticospinal), inferior oliveMedial lemniscus (vertical, beside the midline), spinothalamic (lateral), XII nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract4th ventricle, vagal nuclei, nucleus solitarius
Medulla (closed, lower)Pyramidal decussationSpinothalamic, spinal trigeminalGracile and cuneate nuclei and fasciculi; sensory decussation (internal arcuate fibres)
  • MLF (medial longitudinal fasciculus) links III, IV and VI nuclei: damage (MS) → internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
  • Rule of 4s for brainstem syndromes: 4 midline structures start with M (motor tract, medial lemniscus, MLF, motor nuclei III, IV, VI, XII)
    • 4 lateral ones with S (spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, sensory V nucleus, sympathetic).

los.text: Identify the pathway of the corticospinal tract from the pre-central gyrus to the anterior horn cell and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along that pathway.
los.html:
1Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex, Betz cells; leg medially, face laterally).
2. Corona radiataPosterior limb of the internal capsule.
3. Cerebral peduncle(midbrain)Basilar pons → medullary pyramid.
4. Pyramidal decussation(~85–90% cross)Lateral corticospinal tract (the rest: anterior corticospinal tract, cross at their level).
5Synapse on the anterior horn cell (lower motor neuron) → muscle.
Lesion siteEffect
Motor cortex (e.g. MCA stroke)Contralateral weakness of face and arm more than leg (ACA: leg)
Internal capsule (lacunar)Dense contralateral hemiplegia (face, arm, leg equally)
BrainstemContralateral hemiplegia + ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy (crossed signs, e.g. Weber's)
Spinal cord (above the anterior horn)Ipsilateral UMN weakness below the lesion
Anterior horn / nerveLMN signs at that level
UMN signsLMN signs
Spasticity (clasp-knife), hyperreflexia, upgoing plantar (Babinski), clonus, no wasting early, pyramidal pattern (extensors weak in arms, flexors in legs)Flaccid, hyporeflexia, wasting, fasciculations, downgoing plantar

los.text: Identify the routes of the two principal sensory pathways from the dorsal root ganglion to the thalamus and parietal lobe and link to the functional consequences of damage at different points along that pathway.
los.html:
Dorsal column–medial lemniscusSpinothalamic (anterolateral)
ModalitiesFine touch, vibration, proprioceptionPain, temperature, crude touch
1st neuronDRG → up the dorsal column on the same side (gracile: legs, medial; cuneate: arms, lateral)DRG → synapse in the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa)
CrossesMedulla (internal arcuate fibres) after synapsing in the gracile/cuneate nucleiSpinal cord, within 1–2 segments (anterior white commissure)
2nd neuronMedial lemniscus → thalamusSpinothalamic tract → thalamus
3rd neuronVPL → postcentral gyrus (parietal lobe)VPL → postcentral gyrus
Lesion siteEffect
Hemisection (Brown-Séquard)Same side: proprioception/vibration loss and weakness; opposite side: pain and temperature loss (from 1–2 levels below)
Central cord (syringomyelia)Cape-like bilateral pain and temperature loss (crossing fibres); dorsal columns spared
Dorsal columns (B12 deficiency, tabes dorsalis)Lost vibration and proprioception; sensory ataxia, positive Romberg's
Anterior spinal arteryWeakness and pain/temperature loss; dorsal columns spared
Above the medulla (brainstem, thalamus, cortex)All sensation lost on the opposite side
ThalamusContralateral loss; thalamic pain syndrome
Parietal cortexContralateral loss of fine discrimination (astereognosis, two-point), neglect (non-dominant)

los.text: Recognise the normal brainstem and cerebellum, and common pathology on radiological images.
los.html:
ImagingNormal featuresCommon pathology
CT (first in acute stroke, trauma)
  • Brainstem and cerebellum in the posterior fossa
  • 4th ventricle (CSF dark) in front of the cerebellum
  • Streak artefact from the petrous bones limits detail
Cerebellar haemorrhage (bright: surgical emergency if >3 cm or hydrocephalus); infarct (dark, often missed early on CT); hydrocephalus (dilated ventricles)
MRI (best for the posterior fossa)Midbrain (peduncles, aqueduct), pons (bulging basilar part), medulla (pyramids, olives); cerebellar hemispheres, vermis, folia; tonsils above the foramen magnum
  • Posterior circulation stroke (bright on diffusion-weighted imaging)
  • MS plaques
  • Vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle
  • Chiari malformation (tonsils >5 mm below foramen magnum)
  • Tumours (medulloblastoma in children, metastases, haemangioblastoma)
  • Warning sign: a swollen cerebellum (infarct or bleed) compresses the 4th ventricle (obstructive hydrocephalus) and the brainstem (coning).
